name: Huave
confidence_why: Belmar 1901 puts stress on the last syllable, and every later first-hand description agrees for all Huave varieties (Kim 2008 for San Francisco del Mar, Salminen 2016 for San Dionisio del Mar, and Noyer 2012's own Santa María del Mar forms and remarks); the one open question is which village Belmar recorded, Santa María del Mar according to Noyer 2012 and Salminen 2016 but San Francisco del Mar a…
catalog_citation: Belmar, Francisco. 1901. Estudio del huave (Lenguas del Estado de Oaxaca). Oaxaca. Section 'Acento', p. 27; definition of the grave-accented ì in the vowel section, p. 18.
catalog_locator: printed p. 27, section ACENTO (= pdf page 34 of the archive.org scan lenguasdelestad00belmgoog; page image the copy we hold, header '—27—'; archive.org DjVu scanned); printed p. 18 (= pdf page 25; page image the copy we hold rendered during this reading, header '—18—'; scanned)
catalog_quote: El Huave difiere en cuanto al acento tónico de las demás lenguas del Estado en que estas tienen diferentes acentos que hacen difícil la pronunciación genuina de las voces. Por regla general el acento en las palabras huaves carga en la última sílaba. Como: angót, bastón. niuchúk, batidor. tsatsohón, chacotear. akás, cuanto. Si la palabra termina en vocal muda el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba. Como: assoóitì, culpa. shíkì, yo. ndohkì, degollar. [p. 18: La ì con acento grave es semi-muda, y da á la consonante que la precede su sonido fuerte. Ejemplos: achichì, acedarse. nanvuinkì, alisar. ikihchì, atusar. mitoitì, cadera, &.]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Por regla general el acento en las palabras huaves carga en la última sílaba. Como: angót, bastón. niuchúk, batidor. tsatsohón, chacotear. akás, cuanto. Si la palabra termina en vocal muda el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba. Como: assoóiti, culpa. shíki, yo. ndohki, degollar.
new_statements.translation: As a general rule the accent in Huave words falls on the last syllable. E.g.: angót 'staff', niuchúk 'beater', tsatsohón 'to joke', akás 'how much'. If the word ends in a mute vowel the accent falls on the penultimate syllable. E.g.: assoóiti 'fault', shíki 'I', ndohki 'to behead'.
new_statements.citation: Belmar, Francisco. 1901. Estudio del huave (Lenguas del Estado de Oaxaca). Oaxaca. Section 'Acento', p. 27.
new_statements.locator: p. 27 (section ACENTO; pdf page 34 of the archive.org scan lenguasdelestad00belmgoog; page image saved)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (Google scan, 125 pp., no text layer) and the saved page image printed p. 27 = pdf p. 34; page header '—27—' visible). The section 'ACENTO.' is there and reads: 'El Huave difiere en cuanto al acento tónico de las demás lenguas del Estado en que estas tienen diferentes acentos que hacen difícil la pronunciación genuina de las voces. Por regla general el acento en las palabras huaves carga en la última sílaba. Como: angót, bastón. niuchúk, batidor. tsatsohón, chacotear. akás, cuanto. Si la palabra termina en vocal muda el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba. Como: assoóitì, culpa. shíkì, yo. ndohkì, degollar.' The reported quote matches word for word ex…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the final syllable; words ending in a 'mute' (reduced/epenthetic) vowel are stressed on the penult, i.e. on the last full syllable. Consistent with the modern descriptions of the sister dialects (Kim 2008: fixed final stress in San Francisco del Mar; Noyer 2013: final if closed, else penult in San Mateo del Mar) and with the Santa María del Mar verb forms Noyer 2013 prints with final stress (SMa t-a-moᵑɡ+ós, m-a-ⁿʦ′om+ó:s, mokʷik+í:əs).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Belmar. Kim 2008 (San Francisco del Mar) finds no case for secondary stress; Noyer 2013 (San Mateo) has cyclic secondary stress in derived words. Nothing for Santa María del Mar.
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in a mute vowel take penultimate stress (Belmar). For the sister dialects: open-final function words and Spanish loans take penult stress (Noyer 2013, San Mateo). Noyer 2013 §1.3.3 states that Santa María del Mar, unlike San Mateo, has no lexical tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (isolated words in a 19th-century grammar). Belmar does not identify the village his data come from; attribution to Santa María del Mar rests only on Romero Delgado 2014 §5.3.4, contradicted by Montero Gutenberg 2017 p. 132 (San Francisco del Mar) and Kim 2008 p. 7 (listed among old San Mateo sources).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Belmar 1901) describes 'Huave' without naming the village; Belmar lists all five settlements including Santa María del Mar (p. 1) but never says where his informants were from. Romero Delgado 2014 (§5.3.4, p. 94) treats Belmar 1901/1905 as the Santa María del Mar monographs; Montero Gutenberg 2017 (p. 132) judges from the examples that they reflect San Francisco del Mar; Kim 2008 (p. 7) lists Belmar 1901 among older San Mateo del Mar [sanm1287] sources. The only certainly-Santa María data opened are Noyer 2013's SMa verb forms (final stress marked; no tone), which support the same reading but contain no explicit rule. The Santa María-specific descriptions (Suárez 1975; Noyer s/f Umbeyujts sketch) were not accessible.

new_statements.quote: [p. xviii] En los datos de Radin, se escribe [ˈ] antes de la sílaba (o sílabas) con acento primario, y se escribe [ˌ] antes de una sílaba con acento secundaria. Sin embargo, en el caso regular en que es la última sílaba que lleva el acento primario, se suprime el signo. [p. 11, entry AN] En SMo y SD el enclítico ni cambia la posición del acento fonético del tema al que se añade ni lleva su propio acento; en SMa normalmente ambos la sílaba final del tema y el enclítico llevan su propio acento fonético de fuerza casi igual.
new_statements.translation: [p. xviii] In Radin's data, [ˈ] is written before the syllable (or syllables) with primary stress, and [ˌ] before a syllable with secondary stress. However, in the regular case in which it is the last syllable that carries primary stress, the mark is suppressed. [p. 11, entry AN] In San Mateo and San Dionisio the enclitic neither changes the position of the phonetic stress of the stem it attaches to nor carries its own stress; in Santa María del Mar normally both the final syllable of the stem and the enclitic carry their own phonetic stress of almost equal force.
new_statements.citation: Noyer, Rolf. 2012. Diccionario etimológico y comparativo de las lenguas huaves (Nadam minawijk mipuoch Umbeyajts, San Dionisio del Mar; Nadam minawij mipuch Umbeyüjts, Santa María del Mar; Nadam minawij mipoch Umbeyajts, San Francisco del Mar; Nadam minawiig mipoch Ombeayiiüts, San Mateo del Mar). Ms., University of Pennsylvania, August 2012 version, 1024 pp.
new_statements.locator: Introducción, p. xiii (pdf page 14, siglum R) and 'Acento y tono', p. xviii (pdf page 19); dictionary entry AN, p. 11 (pdf page 79)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: pdf page 19 (header 'xviii', section 'Acento y tono') verbatim: 'En los datos de Radin, se escribe [ˈ] antes de la sílaba (o sílabas) con acento primario, y se escribe [ˌ] antes de una sílaba con acento secundaria. Sin embargo, en el caso regular en que es la última sílaba que lleva el acento primario, se suprime el signo.' Same page: 'En SMa, al menos para algunos hablantes, se neutralizan los contrastes entre [i e], [u o] y [ɨ a] en sílabas atónicas'. pdf page 79 (header 'AN 11') verbatim: 'En SMo y SD el enclítico ni cambia la posición del acento fonético del tema al que se añade ni lleva su propio acento; en SMa normalmente ambos la sílaba final del tema y el enclítico llevan su propio…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing final-stress statement (Belmar 1901): the 'regular case' is final primary stress, and the one Santa María-specific remark presupposes a stressed stem-final syllable; it adds the enclitic-stress detail and unstressed-vowel neutralisation for Santa María. Noyer also codes every Belmar 1901 form as Santa María del Mar (p. ii: 'La gramática y vocabulario del huave de Santa María del Mar por Francisco Belmar, publicado en 1901 (sigla B)'). Note the regular-final-stress sentence is written about Radin's San Dionisio notes, not about Santa María directly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The regular case across the Huave varieties is primary stress on the last syllable (so regular final stress goes unmarked in the transcriptions); for Santa María del Mar specifically the only remark is that the enclitic =an carries its own stress nearly equal to the stem-final stress, i.e. the stem still ends in a stressed syllable. Unstressed-syllable vowel neutralisation ([i e], [u o], [ɨ a]) is reported for some Santa María speakers (p. xviii). No explicit stress rule is stated for Santa María del Mar as such.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Radin's notation allows a secondary-stress mark [ˌ], but no rule for secondary stress is given; in Santa María del Mar both stem-final syllable and enclitic =an are said to bear near-equal stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitic =an is stressless in San Mateo and San Dionisio but stressed (near-equal) in Santa María del Mar; Noyer's own Santa María forms (siglum Ma RN) are marked for stress only where non-final, e.g. [kanaˈen+ˈan], [ˈm′aw+ˈan], [n′iŋgɨy-an].
new_statements.identity_note: Salminen 2016 describes the San Dionisio del Mar variety (Umbeyajts), not Santa María del Mar; its final-stress rule is for that sister variety. Noyer 2012 is comparative over all four Huave villages; its general final-stress sentence is written about Radin's pre-1914 San Dionisio data, and its one Santa María-specific remark is the enclitic-stress note in entry AN (siglum SMa). Both works treat Belmar 1901 as Santa María del Mar data.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on placement: Belmar 1901 (catalog statement, final stress, penult before a 'mute' final vowel that Belmar's own p. 18 defines as the palatalisation mark), Salminen 2016 (San Dionisio: final syllable of the phonological word), Noyer 2012 (regular case = last syllable; Santa María enclitic =an near-equally stressed) all point to final stress. The only disagreement concerns which dialect Belmar 1901 describes: Noyer 2012 (p. ii) and Salminen 2016 (p. 6) attribute it to Santa María del Mar, whereas our earlier reading found Montero Gutenberg 2017 (p. 132) judging it San Francisco del Mar and Kim 2008 (p. 7) listing it among San Mateo del Mar sources. Neither work opened here states an explicit stress rule for Santa María del Mar in its own words.

sources.citation: Kim, Yuni. 2008. Topics in the phonology and morphology of San Francisco del Mar Huave. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. 371 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: San Francisco del Mar only: §2.1.5 pp. 35-36 'there is fixed final stress.. Primary stress falls on the final syllable of each word regardless of morphological constituency'; no case for secondary stress or weight; cued by pitch. On Santa María del Mar it says only that this dialect 'bears the most affinities to San Francisco' (p. 3) and that 'Suárez (1975) is still essentially the only source on the Santa María del Mar dialect' (p. 7).
